<meta>Kangxi imperial Peking woodblock edition of the Mongolian Kanjur (1718–1720), printed in vermilion ink in pothi format; Volume 49 (Ratnakūṭa / Čogčalagsan, vol. 2), folio 2a (recto), opening section of the Ārya-anantamukhapariśodhananirdeśaparivarta-nāma-mahāyānasūtra (無邊莊嚴會).</meta>

<margin>ᠳᠡᠳ ᠴᠣᠭᠴᠠᠯᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠳᠦ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ (ded čogčalagsan degedü qoyar)</margin>
<margin>大寶積經第二卷上二</margin>

᠀ ᠡᠶᠢᠨ ᠬᠡᠮᠡᠨ ᠮᠢᠨᠤ ᠄
ᠰᠣᠨᠣᠰᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠠᠨᠤ ᠃ ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ
ᠴᠠᠭ ᠲᠤᠷ ᠢᠯᠠᠵᠤ ᠲᠡᠭᠦᠰ ᠨᠥᠭᠴᠢᠭᠰᠡᠨ
ᠪᠤᠷᠬᠠᠨ ᠬᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠤ ᠬᠣᠲᠠᠨ ᠳᠤᠷ
ᠭᠠᠳᠷᠢᠭ ᠠᠭᠤᠯᠠ ᠳᠤᠷ ᠄ ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠠᠶᠢᠮᠠᠭ
ᠲᠣᠶᠢᠳ ᠤᠨ ᠮᠢᠩᠭᠠᠨ ᠨᠠᠶᠢᠮᠠᠨ
ᠵᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠲᠣᠶᠢᠳ ᠯᠤᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠬᠠᠮᠲᠤ
ᠨᠢᠭᠡᠨ ᠡ ᠰᠠᠭᠤᠨ ᠪᠦᠯᠡᠭᠡ ᠄ ᠲᠡᠳᠡᠭᠡᠷ
ᠪᠦᠭᠦᠳᠡ ᠪᠡᠷ ᠳᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠢ ᠳᠠᠷᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠃
ᠴᠤᠪᠤᠷᠢᠯ ᠪᠠᠷᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠃ ᠨᠢᠰᠸᠠᠨᠢᠰ ᠦᠭᠡᠢ
ᠪᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠡᠷᠬᠡ ᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠃
ᠰᠡᠳᠬᠢᠯ ᠮᠠᠰᠢᠳᠠ ᠲᠡᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ ᠲᠣᠨᠢᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠃
ᠪᠢᠯᠢᠭ ᠮᠠᠰᠢᠳᠠ ᠲᠡᠶᠢᠨ ᠪᠦᠭᠡᠳ
ᠲᠣᠨᠢᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠰᠠᠶᠢᠨ ᠮᠣᠷᠢᠨ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ
ᠶᠡᠬᠡ ᠵᠠᠭᠠᠨ ᠮᠡᠲᠦ ᠃ ᠦᠶᠢᠯᠡᠳᠪᠦᠷᠢ
ᠶᠢ ᠦᠶᠢᠯᠡᠳᠦᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠦᠶᠢᠯᠡᠰ ᠢ ᠪᠦᠲᠦᠭᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ
ᠠᠴᠢᠭᠠᠨ ᠢᠶᠠᠨ ᠭᠡᠭᠡᠭᠰᠡᠨ ᠃
ᠥᠪᠡᠷ ᠦᠨ ᠲᠤᠰᠠ ᠶᠢ ᠣᠯᠤᠭᠰᠠᠨ
ᠰᠠᠨᠰᠠᠷ ᠤᠨ ᠪᠠᠷᠢᠯᠳᠤᠯᠭ᠎ᠠ ᠃ ᠪᠠᠷᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠃
ᠦᠨᠡᠨ ᠮᠡᠳᠡᠯ ᠢᠶᠡᠷ ᠰᠡᠳᠬᠢᠯ ᠮᠠᠰᠢᠳᠠ

translation.text:
<meta>Kangxi imperial Peking woodblock edition of the Mongolian Kanjur from 1718 to 1720, printed in vermilion ink in pothi format; Volume 49, Ratnakūṭa or Čogčalagsan, volume 2, folio 2a recto, opening section of the Ārya-anantamukhapariśodhananirdeśaparivarta-nāma-mahāyānasūtra, the Assembly of Boundless Adornment. Header and signature: Second Volume of the Heap of Jewels, Great Heap of Jewels Sutra, Volume Two, Upper Two, folio 2a.</meta>

<note>A rectangular double-ruled woodblock border printed in vermilion red ink features a continuous foliate scrollwork frame. Vertical marginal ear-boxes on the left and right ends contain the Mongolian and Chinese volume and folio signatures, each flanked at the top and bottom by small floral scroll panels.</note>

<margin>Second Volume of the Heap of Jewels, Upper Two <note>original: "ᠳᠡᠳ ᠴᠣᠭᠴᠠᠯᠠᠭᠰᠠᠨ ᠳᠡᠭᠡᠳᠦ ᠬᠣᠶᠠᠷ / ded čogčalagsan degedü qoyar", the Mongolian marginal signature for the Ratnakūṭa section, volume 2, folio 2 recto</note></margin>
<margin>Great Heap of Jewels Sutra, Volume Two, Upper Two <note>original: "大寶積經第二卷上二", the Chinese marginal signature for the Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra, volume 2, folio 2 recto</note></margin>

Thus have I <note>original: "᠀ eyin kemen minu :"; the opening head-mark marks the start of the sutra</note>
heard: At one <note>original: "sonosugsan anu : nigen", completing the standard Buddhist sutra opening formula translating Sanskrit evaṃ mayā śrutam</note>
time, the Victoriously Transcendent Accomplished <note>original: "čag-tur ilaju tegüs nögčigsen", the standard Mongolian calque of Tibetan bcom ldan 'das for Sanskrit Bhagavān, the Blessed One</note>
<term>burqan</term> <gloss>Buddha, the Awakened One</gloss> was in the City of the King <note>original: "burqan qayan-u qotan-dur"; "City of the King" is the calque for Sanskrit Rājagṛha, the capital of Magadha</note>,
on Mount <term>Gadrig</term> <gloss>Vulture Peak, Sanskrit Gṛdhrakūṭa</gloss>, with a great assembly <note>original: "gadrig ayula-dur : yeke ayimag"</note>
of <term>toyid</term> <gloss>Buddhist monks, Sanskrit bhikṣu</gloss>, one thousand eight <note>original: "toyid-un mingyan nayiman"</note>
hundred monks in all, <note>original: "jayun toyid-luy-a qamtu"</note>
dwelling together in one place. Those monks <note>original: "nigen-e sayun bülege : tedeger"</note>
had all conquered the foe <note>original: "bügüde-ber dayin-i darugsan :", a calque of Tibetan dgra bcom pa for Sanskrit arhat, a worthy one who has destroyed the enemy of the afflictions</note>.
They had exhausted contaminations <note>original: "čuburil baraysan :", translating Sanskrit kṣīṇāsrava, having ended all mental outflows</note>, and were free of <term>nisvanis</term> <gloss>mental afflictions or passions, Sanskrit kleśa</gloss>, <note>original: "nisvanis ügei"</note>
having come to attain self-mastery <note>original: "bolugsan erke olugsan :", translating Sanskrit vaśībhūta</note>.
Their minds were thoroughly and completely liberated <note>original: "sedkil masida teyin büged tonilugsan :", translating Sanskrit suvimuktacitta</note>.
Their wisdom was thoroughly and completely <note>original: "bilig masida teyin büged", translating Sanskrit suvimuktaprajña</note>
liberated. They were like noble thoroughbred steeds <note>original: "tonilugsan sayin morin metü", literally "like a good horse", translating Sanskrit ājāneya</note>,
and like great elephants <note>original: "yeke jayan metü :", translating Sanskrit mahānāga</note>. Their work <note>original: "üyiledbüri"</note>
was done, and their tasks were accomplished <note>original: "yi üyiledügsen üyiles-i bütügegsen", translating Sanskrit kṛtakṛtya kṛtakaraṇīya</note>.
They had laid down their burden <note>original: "ačiyan-iyan gegegsen :", translating Sanskrit apahṛtabhāra</note>.
They had attained their own highest good <note>original: "öber-ün tusa-yi olugsan", literally "obtained their own benefit", translating Sanskrit anuprāptasvakārtha</note>,
and had exhausted the fetters of <term>sansar</term> <gloss>cyclic existence, Sanskrit saṃsāra</gloss> <note>original: "sansar-un barilduly-a : baraysan :", translating Sanskrit parikṣīṇabhavasaṃyojana</note>.
Through true knowledge, their minds were thoroughly <note>original: "ünen medel-iyer sedkil masida"; the sentence breaks off at the end of folio 2a and continues onto folio 2b to complete the formula corresponding to Sanskrit samyagājñāsuvimuktacitta, "their minds were thoroughly liberated through right knowledge"</note>

<note>This page contains twenty vertical lines of classical Mongolian printed from left to right across the recto leaf, flanked by Mongolian and Chinese volume signatures in the left and right marginal ear-boxes.</note>

<summary>This folio recto from Volume 49 of the Kangxi imperial woodblock edition of the Mongolian Kanjur presents the opening lines of the Sutra Teaching the Purification of Boundless Gateways, the second assembly of the Great Heap of Jewels collection. It records the setting of the teaching on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, where the Buddha resides with one thousand eight hundred arhat monks whose spiritual accomplishments are praised through classical Buddhist epithets.</summary>
<keywords>Mongolian Kanjur, Mahāratnakūṭa, Heap of Jewels, Rājagṛha, Vulture Peak, Gṛdhrakūṭa, Buddha, arhat, monastic assembly, spiritual liberation, Kangxi woodblock edition</keywords>
